processing: Little is recorded for this tea; Dancong in general is withered, tossed for partial oxidation, fixed, rolled and dried.
harvest_season: Usually spring, as with most Fenghuang Dancong.
appearance_dry: Typically straight, dark yellow-brown strips, as with other Dancong.
appearance_liquor: Orange-yellow, as usually described for the Zhi Lan aroma type.
appearance_wet: Typically thick leaves with reddened edges, as with other tossed Dancong.
taste_profile: No detailed tasting record is known; the Zhi Lan type it belongs to is generally described as elegant orchid with a lasting aroma and a clear sweet return.

brewing.notes: General Dancong advice: plenty of leaf, hot water, quick pours.

vintage_note: Little is known about how this particular name is sold. Dancong as a class goes by harvest year and season, usually fresh spring tea or tea rested a year or two after roasting.
description:
Zhongping Zhilan is a Fenghuang Dancong whose name joins a place, Zhongping, with an aroma type, Zhi Lan. Little else about it is recorded, so what follows is mostly about the class.

Dancong is generally made by withering and tossing the leaf for partial oxidation, followed by fixing, rolling and drying.

Zhi Lan is one of the ten recognised Dancong aroma types, generally described as elegant, lasting orchid with a clear sweet return. How closely this tea fits that picture needs tasting rather than assumption.

The name rarely appears for sale. If you meet it, ask where Zhongping lies relative to the seller's gardens and which tree the leaf comes from.
history: Little is documented. Chinese writing on Dancong names cites it as an example of teas named for their place and aroma, alongside Po Tou Zhi Lan. Its exact location on the mountain, its age and who first made it are not recorded in anything widely available.
